notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00541.opp-gr: §3: 'after that great [aid]' fills an ellipsis (μετὰ τὴν μεγάλην ἐκείνην, sc. ἐπικουρίαν). §9: the verse is Hesiod, Works and Days 240. §13: the edition's stray bracket after τοῦτό γε is omitted. §12: <δεῖνα τὸν> is an editorial supplement, translated.

21: the word ἃς before 'those who were sacrificed' appears corrupt and has been left untranslated. 31: the text 'οὐκ δίεις μὴ λάχῃ; τέ οὖν' is garbled; it is read as 'οὐκ ᾔδεις μὴ λάχῃ; τί οὖν', and the sense is uncertain. 27: the first λοιμοὺς is read as λοιμὸν, 'the plague'. 30: the sentence about harming 'a whole household and city' is obscure. 'City' has been taken as the object of the following clause.

36.2: "ἴ’ ἀφάνισον" read as ἢ ἀφάνισον ("or hide"). 38.1: "διὰ ἕν" appears corrupt; translated as a question "why should he..." (διὰ τί, or the like). 39: the words in angle brackets are an editorial supplement. 41: the bracketed [εἰπεῖν] is deleted by the editor but is translated as "saying". 42: the impious archer who drew his bow against the god is unnamed (perhaps Eurytus, who challenged Apollo).
49.1: τὴν πάλιν is read as τὴν πόλιν ("the city"); ἀστρατείας γραφή is the Athenian legal charge of failing to serve on campaign.

nodes.text: XLI.

A plague gripped the city. The god declared that the plague would cease if the people sacrificed the child of one of the citizens. The lot fell on the son of the magus. He promises to end the plague if they spare the boy. They deliberate.

What seems remarkable to me, citizens, is not that this man is trying by every means to snatch his own son away, but that you, while the city is sick, sit listening to such speeches. For it was the part of people with sense, who wished to end the evil, to obey at once what came from the god, and for no one either to say or to hear anything contrary to it. But since you have abandoned helping the city and put up with long speeches, and someone has had such power among you that he has brought you to inquire whether you ought to neglect a salvation that is plain before you and wait for things that will never happen anywhere, how could you not reasonably be thought out of your minds?

For my part, I thought it right that from his very first words you should at once throw out this polluted wretch and not need an orator against him, but that the people should do the work cleanly by themselves. But since, I do not know how, so much time has been given to this man's lying, and you have needed someone to instruct you on the one matter that needs no instruction at all, I have come forward so as not to allow the magus to be thought better than the Pythian [god].

3. Now, to expose this man's boasting is easy not only for me but for anyone, so lacking in all credibility were the things he has promised; but two things, citizens, in the magus's harangue distress me most: one, that many of the citizens, spellbound now by this man's words—and he is the cause of these things too—are dying while the plague does its work; the other, that the god will no longer be equally willing to help us. For that we should look to other hopes and accept speeches about some other aid after that great [aid of his]—I would be amazed if this did not take away a great part of the goodwill and zeal the god has shown toward the city.

Therefore we must both hate and punish this man severely, since by what he announces and says he will give he robs us of so great a turn in our favour; and I think that those who have spoken in his support too—and it is not unclear why they love the magus—would reasonably meet with your anger, if they place their relations with such a man before the interests of the city.

5. Now some others are at a loss, and have often asked among themselves from what beginning, taking its cause from where, this terrible and unbearable disease is emptying the city. And indeed I heard some lamenting to one another in the marketplace: 'For what wrongdoing are we paying this penalty? Have not temples and shrines and sacred precincts and altars and everything been preserved for the gods according to the ancient laws? Do we not sacrifice? Do we not pour libations? Do we not perform the rites? Do we not hold festivals? Do we not go to battle with their sanction? Do we not bring offerings after victories? Do we not keep treaties? Do we not abide by oaths? Do we not deal justly with our neighbours? How then are we sick?'

That is what the others [say]; but I have never thought it surprising that we suffer what we suffer—not because I condemn the city's ways or am aware of anything impious in you or anything savage (may I never so misjudge the city), but because I see this man unwilling to live by farming or the sea or any other decent occupation, pursuing instead this wicked art, and claiming to know the gods beyond others, and their secrets, and what they delight in, and by what they are drawn, and what they would give in return for what they receive.

In short, the accursed man, calling himself a companion and friend of the gods and promising to resolve every difficulty through them, has overturned many households, hiring himself out to the citizens' enmities, and rolling about among the tombs and from there bringing destruction on people who had done him no wrong, troubling the dead and not letting souls remain in their own abodes.

And many have destroyed those who had offended them through this single hireling, who, by the very evils with which he had already entangled many, was also securing for himself immunity from paying the penalty. For whoever perceived it and was able to judge would advise himself to keep silent, since it was not safe to provoke a man whose power came from graves—indeed I myself now know what I shall suffer, but I have stood up placing the common safety before my own. And it was not only this that fought on his side: those who owed him these fine favours were ready to do and suffer anything for him. And you see how even now they shrink from nothing.

9. Seeing these things, the gods, hating him and pitying those who had fallen into his hands, let loose their anger on all, as has happened often in many places. Nor, it seems, did this escape the noble poets, but they sing knowingly: 'Often even a whole city suffers for a bad man.' This it is that has split the earth open beneath cities, this has brought the sea upon them, this rain beyond measure, this famine, this what [has come] upon us.

But from those who gave the wound comes the remedy too. For when many had already died and the doctors' efforts were nothing, we looked where we ought to look, to the one who has freed not a few cities from both these and many other calamities, the god at Delphi. And I was afraid, I was afraid, citizens, that because we had not driven this man out of the city we would fail to get an oracle; but the god, in his kindness, proves better than my hope, and gives a response clear and simple, not like most Delphic ones that lead some to think this and others that, but he said expressly that if the child of one of the citizens were sacrificed by the people, the evil would stop.

Having heard this, the envoys came back running, pressing on night and day alike, and we sat trembling over what they would come bringing. When we saw them approaching, many of us poured out before the walls and asked whether they had come having heard anything that would let the city breathe again; and when they promised good news, we thought we should not delay, but there was a rush to the assembly, and the secretary at once read out the oracle.

At that point it did not seem right to propose a decree [naming] so-and-so the son of so-and-so—for that, I think, would not have befitted a democracy—but the occasion called for a lot, and in this way equality was preserved.

With the fathers present, and the names of their children lying among the lots, and the next steps carried out, the lot fell on the son of this man who has done many terrible things. And applause followed, as you know, because we were going to be rid of two evils, the plague and a wicked seed.

What was just, then, was that the victim should have been sacrificed at once and the disease gone, and that the city should now be at its second sacrifices, those for its deliverance, and that this man should preferably not grieve too much, since some honour was accruing to him too—or if that was not possible, at least pretend. But he takes up war against the god and despises you, and by what he says prolongs the disease: 'Pay no attention to the Pythian,' he says, 'but to me. For I will end the plague. And why need the boy be sacrificed?' The sorcerer says this, and you put up with it.

Now, you accursed man, you say this, and dare to admit that you were able to help but did not want to? Then it is not the boy who for that reason deserves to live, but this man who deserves to be sacrificed along with the boy; and it is just that the one serve the oracle and the other pay the penalty, since seeing the city perishing so pitifully he neither pitied nor helped it, though he had the power, as he himself says.

15. But this is not worth charging him with, for he has no such power, either then or now; he is putting you off and trying to lead you astray, and is wicked in every way. First, he does not let you abide by what has been decided. Come, what did you resolve then when deliberating about help? Was it not to dismiss all human beings as inferior to the matter, and to take refuge in the aid stronger than every calamity, the god at Delphi?

And I would not say that there were many speeches about this among you. Rather, so-and-so spoke briefly, no one spoke against him, and the people voted. The envoys were chosen, they went there, they consulted the oracle: what will end the disease? They heard, they returned, they reported: it is possible to be free of disease. Shall we now, then, undo what was decided, and not be ashamed of changes of mind, which bring the greatest reproach on both a man and a city? For in such matters it is impossible to escape the charge of folly, since one cannot be right in both courses when they are opposite; rather, one must admit that one of the two was a mistake.

I am amazed if we hate tyrants because they make the people weak, yet are going to be grateful to this man, who makes himself stronger than what the people have ratified. And if someone had undone a decree drafted about a grant, or about the need to help our neighbours, or about sending for help from them, it would have been an outrage and we would have been indignant.

What are you saying? Is it in vain, then, that we assemble, and listen to speakers, and test what is said, and vote, and go away having made binding what seems right? And shall we now calmly bear the overturning of the resolution by which it was decided to set the oracle against the plague?

And if he had attempted what he is doing now before the envoys set out, even so it would have been an outrage, and this man's words would not have been thought better than the hopes from there. But now that they have gone there and made their request and obtained all they asked for, shall we laugh all this to scorn and admire the magus's offer? And if someone were leading us to another god, not even that would be free of blame, but it would be less than the present error, though it would still have its critics. But now, if we turn to a human being after the god, shall we be doing no wrong?

20. Nor indeed can it be said that we went to an oracle, but not one of those greatly trusted or where the truth is most found. Everyone knows that the Delphic oracle surpasses all oracles in its site, its fame, and its truthfulness in everything. This oracle even tyrants of the barbarians recognised, and they brought and dedicated the finest of what they had; this oracle founded most of the Greek cities; this oracle sufficed for the race of the Greeks in its greatest difficulties.

And it is not now for the first time that its power is being judged; rather, against long time and much experience and common testimony, a man hateful to the gods claims to appear more august. Nor, then, is the manner of the cure new: calamities have already been ended for others by the same means. And the sacrifices are not obscure; even children could tell of them and recount those who sacrificed, those who were sacrificed, and for what they were sacrificed. What, then, is it that persuades [us] to take the magus in place of the god and what comes from him?

22. So then, even if everything yielded completely to this man's art, it would be most absurd to condemn as madness what was just now decided, and to dishonour a god who did not dishonour the city. But that he is lying and cheating, and promising things he falls far short of, is easy to see. For which of you, citizens, can believe that this man, being a citizen, and seeing such destruction and such danger that none of us would be left, and the law of burials disrupted by the number of the dead, would have held back and not revealed himself, but would have let slip an occasion that offered him the chance to be called saviour of the city? For why, you who today contend with the gods, did you not display this power? Was there no glory in the thing? It cannot even be said how great. Or was there no gain for you, if you wanted it? And which of the things you asked for would you have failed to get?

Each of our other benefactors became enviable by receiving one thing; but to you we would have given all of them together: maintenance at public expense, exemption from taxes, much land, a mass of talents, statues everywhere in the city, in colonnades, in gymnasia, in temples. And perhaps someone would have proposed that you share in the mixing-bowls and be hymned with the gods. How then did you choose to deprive yourself, together with the city, of so many goods for yourself, begrudging the city its safety, when you could have gained so much along with the city? Who is so perverse as to flee these things instead of seeking them? Who would not have prayed, if he could achieve this, to die, knowing what inscriptions he would receive for what deeds? But you could have enjoyed them even while alive.

Moreover, one stronger than a plague would also be stronger than a famine. And so he would have ended famines for cities, summoning the rain that does not appear and restraining that which is excessive, and persuading the Seasons to do the earth no harm. Moreover, whoever has power for this could easily rout enemies too, needing no arms, horses or generals. How many trophies, then, have you set up over the enemy?

And yet this too would have been accomplished, if you had any power. For surely you would not have preferred to congratulate those who excel rather than be one of those crowned yourself, and praised even more than they, inasmuch as you would have driven off the enemy silently and without trouble. I have often seen this man haggling with merchants over money, now begging, now grateful to receive. Yet why did he need to trouble the rich, when he could be one of those able to give?

For why did your art not reveal all treasures to you and make all that is now hidden in the earth part of your house? 'Because,' he says, 'each man has practised a different thing, and I understand this one not badly. And that I did not come forward to you or make my offer earlier is because of these men here who envy and slander my art; but now I have been driven to necessity.'

As for me, I think there is no need to teach you, who know it, that through those means too he would have come forward quenching the plague and making himself of greater worth. And about the slander, I say this: who would not have put up with a few words and some abuse, when he was about to prove his revilers to be false accusers? And how would you not rather have choked those who begrudge your power, had you shown that you possessed it for the good of the city? I myself would have been the first to stand up and call them plagues and enemies of the city and demand their punishment. But it was not envy you feared. How could it be? Rather, you knew there was nothing so great in you. That is why you approved of our going to the god.

28. Do not suppose, citizens, that everything these men claim to be able to do is possible for them; some things are, some are not, and some greatly, others very little. For men such as this one cannot remove a calamity, but they can contrive and devise one. For this reason they belong among the hated rather than among those deemed worthy of honours. For they have made no one happy, but many wretched.

Why then is this so? Those daemons who are worse and by nature disposed to do harm delight in what these men do, and help them bring about these terrible things that destroy human beings. With these they set friends at odds, stir up war even against their own kin, scatter wealth, bring poverty, knock out an eye, twist a tongue, make a man deaf, bind feet, maim hands, waste away a body, and much besides, things which how they are able to do, and by what acts or words, this man knows well, but I have not learned, and may I never learn. These, then, are the doings of their band, and this is the work of this fine art.

Let him call himself a friend of the wicked daemons, then; I do not object. But to those from whom come good things for human beings and deliverance from evils, this man is an enemy by that very friendship with the others. For one and the same man cannot have power with both; rather, whoever has done harm through the former has deprived himself of the power to do any good through the latter. They harm one man or two, and, even when their power is at its greatest, a whole household; and the city they damage by being wicked and going unpunished, but by their art and their drugs not at all.

31. And why need I prove from afar his inability to do good, when I can do so from the present case? A man who could not divert the lot rescues a whole city from disease? A man useless to his own son in danger overcomes a plague? Did you not know he might be chosen? Why then do you tremble now that he has been? Or did you fear he would be chosen? Why then did you not act so that he would not be? Or did you not expect it? Where, then, is the wonderful magus?

I pass over the rest. But now I and all these men have hold of your son, and we are about to sacrifice him. Defeat us, rescue his body, snatch him from our hands, or hide the young man in a cloud, make us think we have him when we do not. Do you see how helpless you are, and how, now that you are exposed, you have nothing you can do?

33. What proof do you offer that you will end the plague, when you ask us to let go of what we trust and wait for what cannot be trusted? "Because," he says, "if I had not been firmly convinced that I would be equal to the task, I would not have made the offer. For what would I gain, if the boy is led to the slaughter after all?"

This one thing first, magus: that he does not die today. And you, naturally, will ask for the next day too, and a third, and a fourth, and ten, and twice as many, claiming that of the things that lead to the cure you have some in plenty but others not yet, and that what is not yet apparent has the greater power. You will hold forth about the moon and the days of the month, and in short you will find one thing after another that allows delay. Doing nothing, but always saying that you will do it, is enough to create delays.

This is one gain for him, and not a small one; another, greater or no less, is that in these days many of the citizens will depart before the one chosen by lot. For he thinks that this at least will bring no slight consolation to the boy and to himself, and he supposes that what the plague does while it is not ended will lighten his own misfortune.

And what if he says that he must go round the countryside by night, and that no one else must be present, only his son, who alone is able to take part in such rites, and that if this is not granted, everything will have been done in vain; and if with these words he forces you to hand over his son to him, the city's safety, and then goes off and departs to those who are not well disposed towards us, what shall we do? Tell me. Shall we go after another? And who will put up with it? Or shall we find one?

Then, if the god in his anger makes the matter come to nothing, shall we, by Zeus, send to him again and tell him of the disease and seek a remedy? And he will say: "You most absurd of all men, when you had help ready to hand, when you held the victim in your hands, when you had become masters of being sick no longer, you listened to speeches after oracles. Why then do you play the fool, and, having men better than us, not rid yourselves of your troubles through them?" What shall we do then? We shall blame, by Zeus, those who helped this man, and say that we ought not to have been won over by his tears. But we shall perish none the less.

How then is it not a great misfortune, through the magus' words, both to lose the release now in sight and to have none in its place afterwards? And the danger does not stop there: not even when called upon in some other crisis will <the god> come to our help any more. For why should he rescue pious men from dangers? A fine proof of piety the present affair is! So surely does obeying this man today make the Pythian [god] hostile to us once and for all; and there is no small fear that something else may be added to the plague, and that this too may be incurable for the city, since the hope from Delphi will have been cut off from us.

39. And from this too, citizens, you may learn that you must not heed this man. For I ask him in front of you: will you sacrifice another boy in secret and so defeat the adversary? Who is this boy? Where did you get him? Who gave him, <when> the oracle names <no one>? And how much more just that the one chosen by lot should depart?

Or will you find the cure in another way? But the oracle says that this is the only one. If there were several, the god would not have hidden the abundance of the ways to healing, nor would he have shown himself worse than these physicians who pride themselves on mentioning treatments of many kinds; he would have said, listing them, that by doing this or that, or, by Zeus, another thing, or again something else, or this very thing now pronounced, it would be possible to escape the plague. But you see how, setting everything else aside, he says that help lies in this alone, hunting down these men, I think, as though the origin of the plague also came from them, the father leading the way and starting it, the boy following and trying to imitate him.

41. "Why then," he says, "does he not slaughter me?" Because he thinks the death of your son more terrible for you than your own. And for all human beings grief while one lives is heavier than death. "Why then," he says, "did he not say expressly to sacrifice my son?" Because he knew that you would then slander the oracle, saying: "Citizens, this has been contrived from here. This is the work of the envious, this the work of those who cannot bear my reputation. This is not the god, but those men at Delphi who do everything for silver."

For this reason he did not say the name, but achieved the same by the lot. Or do you think that what befell those drawing lots did not happen so by the god's vote and judgement? Why then do you use force and contend, and imitate some impious archer of old, who the poets say raised his bow against the god? You too now contend against the oracle, with this difference only, that he went mad by himself alone, while you expect the people to do so too. Or is this, citizens, the conduct of sensible men? Does anyone deliberate about what the oracle has pronounced when he ought to carry the deed out, and keep in a plague that he can end, and lend his ears to the words of men after hearing divine oracles, and wish to go home and see his own people sick when he could see them well?

And what will you say to those themselves who lie in their beds, who crowd around the wells, who are in the grip of the evil, who are burning with fever? Surely they have learned what came from the god, and are wondering, naturally, why they have not yet been released. What then will you say to them, still sick, except the magus, and the magus' offers, and how he makes promises, and how he may perhaps do something? And how will you bear the lament of the suffering? You will seem to have valued the sorcerer's son more highly than your own children.

44. I see many of you, citizens, dressed in black, one for a brother, another for a wife, another for a child, another for all of these. Do you wish, then, that those not yet mourning should suffer the same, and that greater griefs be added to those already stricken? No, by the many tombs! Rather, pity those who are sick, and pity those who are not yet. For it will come, it will come, the evil, marching upon all, unless it is halted by the sword. The magus will suffer nothing terrible or pitiable if, along with many fathers, he seeks his own son; nor would he be justified in saying to us: "Save my son, abandon yours." For this is what he asks, even if he avoids the words.

Yet none of this would be needed, if he truly had the power to do what he claims and promises. For what prevented him, tell me, before saying anything, before promising, from joining the cure to the lot, and making the moment of these words the moment of the plague's release, and then in that way preventing the sacrifice, as there would no longer be any need for it?

"But it was not possible so quickly, only over time." Then even if you are going to end it in this way (let us grant it, though it is utterly foolish), you are not giving equal for equal. For how is it equal to see our children healthy at once and to get this very thing after many deaths? And that a citizen of ours should be so indignant if he is to be of some use to the city through his son, how is that tolerable?

Each of these men, if he saw his own son taken by the lot, would perhaps not even have wept; or if he did, he would perhaps have felt some pleasure mixed with the grief, at making such a contribution to the city. But this man is indignant, and will not bear the public service, and reviles the gods, and all but razes the temples. And those who have done us the greatest good would have kept quiet, while he who has spent his life on wicked drugs expects, like some tyrant, the common safety to give way to his own pleasures.

Why? Because of his many trophies, and the captives, and ships, and harbours, and places [won]? And yet even if all this were so, not even then would he have reasonably demanded as his reward that the city should cease to exist. And if you would not have given such an honour to generals, or to the bravest in battle, or to those who rescued us from the greatest dangers, how will you give it to the sorcerer?

You cannot bear the slaughter of your son? But if he had grown to manhood, taken up arms, and fallen fighting for his own [country], would you not have borne it even then? Yet other fathers, at least, buried those who died in this way with pride. And somewhere, too, a general who had led his own sons into battle came back carrying them as corpses, and blamed neither the city, nor himself, nor them. But you would have urged your sons to stay at home, and to face a charge of evading military service rather than endure wounds. Quick indeed this man would have been, if the oracle had called for a father's greatness of spirit, to leap up ahead of the others and offer his son, he who does not even put up with the lot!

50. Now if you were not a magus, I would have consoled you with the words I would use to any other father: "My dearest friend, consider that your son has died in the plague; consider [that he died] before the plague. Reckon how many of his age we carried out [for burial] yesterday. And what if the life after this held for him something still harder than his present end? He departs garlanded, with libation and prayers, leaving behind a great name for himself."

These things, and many like them, I would have gone through, if you were no different from other men; but as it is, hear what your art allows me to say: Why are you afraid, magus? Why do you weep? You will have your son even after the slaughter. He will answer you when you call, he will appear, he will converse with you, he will spend the nights with you; indeed he will probably serve you more eagerly than your other phantoms. So do not be distressed along with the city, when you yourself stand to gain privately.
